title: Time Study

VA.label: Value-added
VA.note: Changes the product or the service in a way the customer pays for.

NVA.label: Necessary
NVA.note: Adds no value but cannot be dropped today: scanning, fetching a box, a required check.

W.label: Waste
W.note: Walking, searching, waiting, rework. Remove it before you buy anything.

over.meaning: A station above takt sets the pace of the whole line: everything upstream waits, everything downstream starves. The line produces at the speed of its slowest station, not at the speed of its best people.
moves: Remove the waste elements of this station first: walking, searching and waiting cost nothing to take out.
Move the last element of this station to the next one with slack, or the first element to the one before it, so the order of the work stays.
Only when the work is balanced and the waste is gone, look at tools, fixtures or automation for the value-added elements that remain.
over.question: What does the operator at this station do while the one next to it waits?

balanced.meaning: Every station is under takt, so the line can meet the demand. The gap between the slowest station and the others is the hidden capacity: the closer the stations are to each other, the fewer operators the line needs.
moves: Take out the waste elements that remain; they are time paid for and not sold.
Watch the variation: a station with a wide spread misses takt on bad cycles even when its median is fine.
Compare the operators needed with the operators you have, then decide where the spare hours go.
balanced.question: Which station would be the bottleneck if the demand rose by ten per cent?

advice.variation: The median of a station is fine, but its cycles vary a lot. Watch five more cycles and write down what is different on the slow ones: a missing box, a long walk, a question to the lead.
advice.waste: More than a fifth of the observed time is waste. The cheapest capacity on this line is in those elements, not in a faster machine.
advice.fewCycles: Fewer than three cycles observed on at least one element. Time three to five more before you change the standard: one cycle shows a moment, not the work.

tips: Stand where you see the hands and the walk. Tell the team what you are timing and why; a hidden stopwatch poisons the next ten studies.
Time the work, not the person.
The standard describes the method at a normal pace. A fast operator and a slow one doing the same method should give you the same elements, not the same seconds.
The median lies less than the mean.
One dropped box or one question to the lead pulls the mean up. The median stays with the typical cycle; the outliers are listed on their own.
Available time divided by demand. A station above takt cannot be fixed by working harder; it needs less work or more hands.
Walking, searching and waiting are waste: remove them first. Scanning and required checks are necessary: shorten them later. Only value-added time deserves automation.
